      "text": "These problems (specifically 8, 10, 11, and 12) all belong to a classic analytical chemistry method called the **Warder Method**. It is used to determine the composition of an alkaline mixture that can contain Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH), Sodium Carbonate ($\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$), and Sodium Bicarbonate ($\\text{NaHCO}_3$).\n\nHere is the step-by-step guide on how to solve any problem of this type.\n\n### Step 1: Understand the Rules of the Mixture\nA stable solution in water **cannot** contain all three of these substances at the same time. This is because strong base (NaOH) and weak acid ($\\text{NaHCO}_3$) react with each other:\n$\\text{NaOH} + \\text{NaHCO}_3 \\rightarrow \\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3 + \\text{H}_2\\text{O}$\n\nTherefore, your solution can only be one of five possibilities:\n1.  NaOH only\n2.  $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$ only\n3.  $\\text{NaHCO}_3$ only\n4. A mixture of **NaOH and $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$**\n5. A mixture of **$\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$ and $\\text{NaHCO}_3$**\n\n### Step 2: Understand the Two Titration Stages\nYou titrate the mixture with a strong acid (HCl) using two different indicators to find two distinct volumes.\n\n*   **$V_1$ (Phenolphthalein endpoint, pH ~8.3):**\n    At this point, all the strong base (NaOH) is neutralized, and the carbonate ($\\text{CO}_3^{2-}$) has been converted to bicarbonate ($\\text{HCO}_3^{-}$). You are exactly halfway done neutralizing the carbonate.\n*   **$V_2$ (Bromocresol green/blue or Methyl orange endpoint, pH ~4.5):**\n    This is the **total volume** of HCl used from the very beginning to neutralize everything completely down to carbonic acid ($\\text{H}_2\\text{CO}_3$). *Note: Problems sometimes word this as taking a fresh aliquot for the second indicator, or just continuing from the first. Either way, $V_2$ represents the total acid needed for full neutralization.*\n\n### Step 3: The Diagnostic \"Cheat Sheet\"\nTo find out what is in your mixture, you compare the relationship between $V_1$ and $V_2$. This is the key to solving every one of these problems:\n\n*   **If $V_1 \u003d V_2$:** Only **NaOH** is present. (Everything reacted at the high pH).\n*   **If $V_1 \u003d 0$ and $V_2 \u003e 0$:** Only **$\\text{NaHCO}_3$** is present. (Nothing reacted at the high pH).\n*   **If $2 \\cdot V_1 \u003d V_2$:** Only **$\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$** is present. (The first half of the neutralization took exactly the same amount of acid as the second half).\n*   **If $V_1 \u003e \\frac{V_2}{2}$:** The mixture is **NaOH + $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$**. (More acid was used in the first step because it had to neutralize NaOH *plus* half the carbonate).\n*   **If $V_1 \u003c \\frac{V_2}{2}$:** The mixture is **$\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$ + $\\text{NaHCO}_3$**. (More acid was used in the second step because it had to neutralize the bicarbonate formed from the carbonate *plus* the bicarbonate that was originally there).\n\n---\n\n### Let\u0027s walk through an example using your images:\n\n**Let\u0027s solve Problem 8:**\n*   $V_{\\text{aliquot}} \u003d 25.00$ mL\n*   $c(\\text{HCl}) \u003d 0.1202$ M\n*   $V_1$ (phenolphthalein) \u003d $16.12$ mL\n*   $V_2$ (bromocresol green) \u003d $32.24$ mL\n\n**1. Determine the composition:**\nLook at the relation between $V_1$ and $V_2$.\n$16.12 \\text{ mL} \\times 2 \u003d 32.24 \\text{ mL}$\nBecause **$2 \\cdot V_1 \u003d V_2$**, we look at our cheat sheet. The solution contains **only $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$**.\n\n**2. Calculate the concentration:**\nSince it\u0027s only $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$, we know that $V_1$ represents exactly *half* of the neutralization (from $\\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ to $\\text{HCO}_3^{-}$). The molar ratio for this half-step is 1:1.\n*   Moles of HCl used for $V_1$: $n(\\text{HCl}) \u003d c \\cdot V \u003d 0.1202 \\text{ mol/L} \\cdot 0.01612 \\text{ L} \u003d 0.0019376$ mol\n*   Moles of $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3 \u003d n(\\text{HCl at } V_1) \u003d 0.0019376$ mol\n*   Concentration of $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$: $c \u003d \\frac{n}{V_{\\text{aliquot}}} \u003d \\frac{0.0019376 \\text{ mol}}{0.025 \\text{ L}} \u003d \\mathbf{0.0775 \\text{ M}}$\n\n---\n\n**Let\u0027s look at how to set up Problem 11 (which is a mixture):**\n*   $c(\\text{HCl}) \u003d 0.1000$ M, $V_{\\text{aliquot}} \u003d 25.00$ mL\n*   $V_1 \u003d 12.00$ mL\n*   $V_2 \u003d 36.00$ mL\n\n**1. Determine composition:**\nIs $12.00 \u003e \\frac{36.00}{2}$ or is $12.00 \u003c \\frac{36.00}{2}$?\n$12.00 \u003c 18.00$. Since **$V_1 \u003c \\frac{V_2}{2}$**, the mixture is **$\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$ + $\\text{NaHCO}_3$**.\n\n**2.         "text": "These problems (specifically 8, 10,"
      }, {
        "text": " 11, and 12) all belong to a classic analytical chemistry method called the **Warder Method**."
      }, {
        "text": " It is used to determine the composition of an alkaline mixture that can contain Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH), Sodium Carbonate ($\\"
      }, {
        "text": "text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$), and Sodium Bicarbonate ($\\text{NaHCO}_3$)."
      }, {
        "text": "\n\nHere is the step-by-step guide on how to solve any problem of this type.\n\n### Step 1: Understand the"
      }, {
        "text": " Rules of the Mixture\nA stable solution in water **cannot** contain all three of these substances at the same time. This"
      }, {
        "text": " is because strong base (NaOH) and weak acid ($\\text{NaHCO}_3$) react with each other:\n$\\"
      }, {
        "text": "text{NaOH} + \\text{NaHCO}_3 \\rightarrow \\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_"
      }, {
        "text": "3 + \\text{H}_2\\text{O}$\n\nTherefore, your solution can only be one of five"
      }, {
        "text": " possibilities:\n1.  NaOH only\n2.  $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3"
      }, {
        "text": "$ only\n3.  $\\text{NaHCO}_3$ only\n4. A mixture of **NaOH and $\\"
      }, {
        "text": "text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$**\n5. A mixture of **$\\text{Na"
      }, {
        "text": "}_2\\text{CO}_3$ and $\\text{NaHCO}_3$**\n\n### Step 2:"
      }, {
        "text": " Understand the Two Titration Stages\nYou titrate the mixture with a strong acid (HCl) using two different indicators to"
      }, {
        "text": " find two distinct volumes.\n\n*   **$V_1$ (Phenolphthalein endpoint, pH ~8.3"
      }, {
        "text": "):**\n    At this point, all the strong base (NaOH) is neutralized, and the carbonate ($\\text{CO"
      }, {
        "text": "}_3^{2-}$) has been converted to bicarbonate ($\\text{HCO}_3^{-}$). You are exactly halfway done"
      }, {
        "text": " neutralizing the carbonate.\n*   **$V_2$ (Bromocresol green/blue or Methyl orange endpoint, pH"
      }, {
        "text": " ~4.5):**\n    This is the **total volume** of HCl used from the very beginning to neutralize everything completely"
      }, {
        "text": " down to carbonic acid ($\\text{H}_2\\text{CO}_3$). *Note: Problems sometimes word this"
      }, {
        "text": " as taking a fresh aliquot for the second indicator, or just continuing from the first. Either way, $V_2$ represents"
      }, {
        "text": " the total acid needed for full neutralization.*\n\n### Step 3: The Diagnostic \"Cheat Sheet\"\nTo find out what is"
      }, {
        "text": " in your mixture, you compare the relationship between $V_1$ and $V_2$. This is the key"
      }, {
        "text": " to solving every one of these problems:\n\n*   **If $V_1 \u003d V_2$:** Only **"
      }, {
        "text": "NaOH** is present. (Everything reacted at the high pH).\n*   **If $V_1 \u003d 0$ and"
      }, {
        "text": " $V_2 \u003e 0$:** Only **$\\text{NaHCO}_3$** is present. (Nothing"
      }, {
        "text": " reacted at the high pH).\n*   **If $2 \\cdot V_1 \u003d V_2$:** Only"
      }, {
        "text": " **$\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$** is present. (The first half of the neutralization took exactly the same"
      }, {
        "text": " amount of acid as the second half).\n*   **If $V_1 \u003e \\frac{V_2}{"
      }, {
        "text": "2}$:** The mixture is **NaOH + $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$**. ("
      }, {
        "text": "More acid was used in the first step because it had to neutralize NaOH *plus* half the carbonate).\n*   **If $V"
      }, {
        "text": "_1 \u003c \\frac{V_2}{2}$:** The mixture is **$\\text{Na}_2\\"
      }, {
        "text": "text{CO}_3$ + $\\text{NaHCO}_3$**. (More acid was used in the second step because it had to neutralize"
      }, {
        "text": " the bicarbonate formed from the carbonate *plus* the bicarbonate that was originally there).\n\n---\n\n### Let\u0027s walk through an example"
      }, {
        "text": " using your images:\n\n**Let\u0027s solve Problem 8:**\n*   $V_{\\text{aliquot}}"
      }, {

        "text": " mL\n\n**1. Determine the composition:**\nLook at the relation between $V_1$ and $V_2$."
      }, {
        "text": "\n$16.12 \\text{ mL} \\times 2 \u003d 32.24 \\"
      }, {
        "text": "text{ mL}$\nBecause **$2 \\cdot V_1 \u003d V_2$**, we look at our cheat"
      }, {
        "text": " sheet. The solution contains **only $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$**.\n\n**2. Calculate the"
      }, {
        "text": " concentration:**\nSince it\u0027s only $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$, we know that"

        "text": " $V_1$ represents exactly *half* of the neutralization (from $\\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ to"

      }, {

      }, {
        "text": "\n\n**1. Determine composition:**\nIs $12.00 \u003e \\frac{36.00"
      }, {

      }, {
        "text": "\n$12.00 \u003c 18.00$. Since **$V_1 \u003c \\frac{V_2"

      }, {

      "text": "You absolutely do not need to memorize it! In fact, relying on a \"cheat sheet\" is a bad idea because if you forget one rule, the whole problem falls apart. \n\nIf you understand the **chemistry** of what is happening in the flask, you can derive the rules yourself on the spot in about 10 seconds. \n\nHere is the logic behind the math. It all comes down to **which reactions happen at which pH**.\n\n### The Three Possible Reactions\nWhen you drop $\\text{HCl}$ (a strong acid) into this mixture, it reacts with the bases in a very specific order:\n\n1.  **Reaction 1 (Strongest base first):** $\\text{HCl} + \\text{NaOH} \\rightarrow \\text{NaCl} + \\text{H}_2\\text{O}$\n2.  **Reaction 2 (Medium base next):** $\\text{HCl} + \\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3 \\rightarrow \\text{NaHCO}_3 + \\text{NaCl}$\n    *(Notice that carbonate ($\\text{CO}_3^{2-}$) only accepts ONE proton here. It becomes bicarbonate).*\n3.  **Reaction 3 (Weakest base last):** $\\text{HCl} + \\text{NaHCO}_3 \\rightarrow \\text{H}_2\\text{CO}_3 + \\text{NaCl}$\n    *(Now the bicarbonate accepts the final proton).*\n\n### The Two Indicators (The Magic Key)\nThe reason we use two indicators is that they change color at different pH levels, which tells us exactly which of those three reactions have finished.\n\n*   **Phenolphthalein ($V_1$) changes color around pH ~8.3.** \n    At this pH, Reactions 1 and 2 are finished. Reaction 3 hasn\u0027t started yet. \n    *What does this mean?* The acid $V_1$ measured **ALL of the $\\text{NaOH}$**, and exactly **HALF of the $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$**. It didn\u0027t touch the original $\\text{NaHCO}_3$ at all.\n*   **Bromocresol / Methyl Orange ($V_2$) changes color around pH ~4.5.**\n    At this pH, all three reactions are 100% finished. \n    *What does this mean?* The acid $V_2$ measured **EVERYTHING**. It neutralized all the $\\text{NaOH}$, both \"halves\" of the $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$, and any original $\\text{NaHCO}_3$.\n\n---\n\n### Deriving the Rules Yourself (No Memorization)\n\nLet\u0027s invent three simple variables to represent the volume of $\\text{HCl}$ needed to neutralize each individual chemical:\n*   $v(\\text{OH})$ \u003d acid needed for $\\text{NaOH}$\n*   $v(\\text{CO}_3)$ \u003d acid needed to fully neutralize $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$ (both steps)\n*   $v(\\text{HCO}_3)$ \u003d acid needed for the original $\\text{NaHCO}_3$\n\nBased on how the indicators work (as explained above), we can write two universal equations:\n1.  **$V_1 \u003d v(\\text{OH}) + \\frac{1}{2} v(\\text{CO}_3)$** \n2.  **$V_2 \u003d v(\\text{OH}) + v(\\text{CO}_3) + v(\\text{HCO}_3)$**\n\nNow, apply the rule that $\\text{NaOH}$ and $\\text{NaHCO}_3$ cannot exist in the same beaker (they react with each other). Let\u0027s see how the \"rules\" naturally appear:\n\n**Scenario A: What if the beaker is ONLY $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$?**\n*   That means $v(\\text{OH}) \u003d 0$ and $v(\\text{HCO}_3) \u003d 0$.\n*   Plug those zeros into our equations:\n    *   $V_1 \u003d \\frac{1}{2} v(\\text{CO}_3)$\n    *   $V_2 \u003d v(\\text{CO}_3)$\n*   *Look at that:* $V_2$ is exactly double $V_1$. You just derived the rule **$2 \\cdot V_1 \u003d V_2$**.\n\n**Scenario B: What if the beaker is a mix of $\\text{NaOH}$ and $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$?**\n*   That means $v(\\text{HCO}_3) \u003d 0$, but the other two are present.\n*   Plug the zero into our equations:\n    *   $V_1 \u003d v(\\text{OH}) + \\frac{1}{2} v(\\text{CO}_3)$\n    *   $V_2 \u003d v(\\text{OH}) + v(\\text{CO}_3)$\n*   Let\u0027s cut $V_2$ in half to compare them: \n    *   $\\frac{V_2}{2} \u003d \\frac{1}{2}v(\\text{OH}) + \\frac{1}{2}v(\\text{CO}_3)$\n*   Now compare $V_1$ to $\\frac{V_2}{2}$: \n    $V_1$ has a *full* $v(\\text{OH})$. $\\frac{V_2}{2}$ only has a *half* $v(\\text{OH})$. \n*   *Look at that:* Therefore, $V_1$ must be bigger than half of $V_2$. You just derived the rule **$V_1 \u003e \\frac{V_2}{2}$**.\n\n**Scenario C: What if the beaker is a mix of $\\text{Na}_2\\text{CO}_3$ and $\\text{NaHCO}_3$?**\n*   That means $v(\\text{OH}) \u003d 0$, but the other two are present.\n*   Plug the zero into our equations:\n    *   $V_1 \u003d \\frac{1}{2} v(\\text{CO}_3)$\n    *   $V_2 \u003d v(\\text{CO}_3) + v(\\text{HCO}_3)$\n*   Let\u0027s cut $V_2$ in half to compare them:\n    *   $\\frac{V_2}{2} \u003d \\frac{1}{2}v(\\text{CO}_3) + \\frac{1}{2}v(\\text{HCO}_3)$\n*   Now compare $V_1$ to $\\frac{V_2}{2}$:\n    Both have $\\frac{1}{2}v(\\text{CO}_3)$. But $\\frac{V_2}{2}$ *also* has the extra $\\frac{1}{2}v(\\text{HCO}_3)$ added to it.\n*   *Look at that:* Therefore, $V_1$ must be smaller than half of $V_2$. You just derived the rule **$V_1 \u003c \\frac{V_2}{2}$**.\n\n### Summary\nIf you get stuck on a test, you don\u0027t need a cheat sheet. Just quickly write down:\n*   **$V_1$ \u003d Strong base + half the carbonate**\n*   **$V_2$ \u003d Everything**\n\nOnce you write that down, you can figure out what is in the mixture simply by looking at the numbers the problem gives you.",

      "text": "This is a fantastic question. The fact that phenolphthalein measures *exactly* half of the carbonate isn\u0027t a random coincidence; it is a direct result of how the carbonate molecule ($CO_3^{2-}$) behaves chemically and the specific pH at which it changes forms.\n\nHere is the \"under the hood\" chemistry of why this happens.\n\n### 1. Carbonate is a \"Two-Step\" Base\nThe carbonate ion ($CO_3^{2-}$) is what chemists call a **diprotic** (or dibasic) species. This means it can accept **two** protons ($H^+$) from the hydrochloric acid, but it does not accept them both at the same time. It happens in two distinct, sequential steps:\n\n*   **Step 1 (The First Half):** $CO_3^{2-} + H^+ \\rightarrow HCO_3^-$ \n    *(Carbonate turns into bicarbonate)*\n*   **Step 2 (The Second Half):** $HCO_3^- + H^+ \\rightarrow H_2CO_3 \\rightarrow H_2O + CO_2$\n    *(Bicarbonate turns into carbonic acid/carbon dioxide)*\n\nBecause it takes one $H^+$ for the first step, and one $H^+$ for the second step, the volume of HCl required for Step 1 is exactly equal to the volume of HCl required for Step 2. \n\n### 2. The pH Levels of the Steps are Far Apart\nBecause the first proton is easy to attach and the second proton is much harder to attach, these two steps happen at very different pH ranges.\n\nWhen you have a solution of purely $Na_2CO_3$, the pH is highly alkaline (usually around pH 11 or 12). As you add HCl, the pH slowly drops as you convert $CO_3^{2-}$ into $HCO_3^-$.\n\nEventually, you reach the exact moment where **100% of the $CO_3^{2-}$ has been converted to $HCO_3^-$**, and **0% has started turning into $H_2CO_3$**. \n\nAt this exact moment, you have a beaker full of pure $NaHCO_3$ (sodium bicarbonate). \nWhat is the pH of a pure $NaHCO_3$ solution? We can calculate it using the pKa values of carbonic acid ($pK_{a1} \\approx 6.4$, $pK_{a2} \\approx 10.3$):\n$$pH \u003d \\frac{pK_{a1} + pK_{a2}}{2} \u003d \\frac{6.4 + 10.3}{2} \u003d \\mathbf{8.35}$$\n\n### 3. The Perfect Match with Phenolphthalein\nThis is where the magic of the indicator comes in. \n\nPhenolphthalein is an indicator that is pink at high pH (alkaline) and turns colorless when the pH drops below **8.3**. \n\nLook at that number! The exact moment phenolphthalein loses its color (pH ~8.3) perfectly matches the exact moment the solution becomes pure bicarbonate (pH 8.35). \n\n**Therefore, when the phenolphthalein turns colorless, the chemistry in the beaker is screaming:** \n*\"Stop! You have exactly finished Step 1. You have attached exactly one proton to every carbonate molecule. You are exactly 50% of the way through neutralizing the carbonate.\"*\n\n### Summary\nTo summarize, it works out perfectly because:\n1. Carbonate takes two equal steps to neutralize.\n2. The exact halfway point of this neutralization naturally creates a pH of ~8.3.\n3. Phenolphthalein happens to be a chemical that changes color at exactly pH 8.3. \n\n*(And just to finish the thought: the second step—turning $HCO_3^-$ into $CO_2$—finishes at a pH around 4.0 to 4.5. That is why we use Bromocresol Green or Methyl Orange for the second indicator, because they change color exactly in that 4.5 range!)*",

      "text": "You are 100% justified in asking that! It is actually **impossible** to solve part (b) exactly as written because the problem is missing a critical piece of information: **the initial volume of the acid mixture**. \n\nIt is also missing the $K_a$ (acid dissociation constant) for the weak acid HA, though for these two specific points, we actually wouldn\u0027t need it anyway. \n\nHere is exactly what is going on, what you *can* solve, and how to prove to your teacher/professor that a number is missing.\n\n### Part (a): 0.00 mL added (You CAN solve this)\nEven without the volume, you can find the starting pH because concentration is intensive (it doesn\u0027t depend on volume).\n\nIn your beaker, you have two acids fighting to give off $H^+$ ions:\n1.  **$0.1200\\text{ M HCl}$ (Strong Acid):** Dissociates 100%. It immediately floods the beaker with $0.1200\\text{ M } H^+$.\n2.  **$0.0800\\text{ M HA}$ (Weak Acid):** Wants to dissociate slightly. However, because the beaker is already packed full of $H^+$ from the strong acid, Le Chatelier\u0027s principle forces the weak acid to stay completely intact. This is called the **Common Ion Effect**. \n\nBecause the strong acid completely suppresses the weak acid, we just ignore the HA entirely for the initial pH.\n*   $[H^+] \\approx 0.1200\\text{ M}$\n*   $pH \u003d -\\log(0.1200) \u003d \\mathbf{0.92}$\n\n### Part (b): 5.00 mL added (Why it\u0027s broken)\nWhen you add the strong base (KOH), it will react with the strongest acid first (the HCl). \n\nYou know exactly how much base you are adding:\n*   $n(OH^-) \u003d 0.1000\\text{ mol/L} \\cdot 5.00\\text{ mL} \u003d \\mathbf{0.500\\text{ mmol}}$\n\nTo find the new pH, you need to subtract this $0.500\\text{ mmol}$ of base from the starting moles of $H^+$ to see how much acid is left over. **This is where you are stuck.**\nTo find the starting moles of $H^+$, you need the formula $n \u003d c \\cdot V$.\n*   $n(H^+_{\\text{initial}}) \u003d 0.1200\\text{ M} \\cdot \\mathbf{V_{\\text{initial}}}$\n\nBecause $V_{\\text{initial}}$ is not given, you cannot calculate the moles, you cannot subtract the base, and you cannot find the new total volume ($V_{\\text{initial}} + 5.00\\text{ mL}$).\n\n### What you should do:\nThis is incredibly common in textbook or exam pdfs.       "text": "Your tutor is **absolutely correct**, and that assumption is not a \"shortcut\" or a cheat—it is the standard, mathematically sound way to solve polyprotic acid problems in chemistry!\n\nHere is why your tutor\u0027s assumption is correct, and exactly how to solve the problem.\n\n### Why do we ignore the other reactions?\nLook closely at the given equilibrium constants ($K_a$ values):\n*   $K_{a1} \u003d 7.11 \\times 10^{-3}$\n*   $K_{a2} \u003d 6.32 \\times 10^{-8}$\n*   $K_{a3} \u003d 4.5 \\times 10^{-13}$\n\nNotice how much smaller each step gets. $K_{a1}$ is roughly **100,000 times larger** than $K_{a2}$. This means the first reaction produces essentially 99.999% of the hydronium ions ($H_3O^+$) in the solution. \n\nThe second and third reactions produce such a microscopic amount of $H_3O^+$ that adding them to the total is like pouring a cup of water into a swimming pool—it doesn\u0027t change the measurable total. If you tried to calculate this without ignoring the latter reactions, you would have to solve a horrific 3rd-degree polynomial equation, only to get the exact same final number!\n\n### How to solve it\nBecause we established that only the first reaction matters, we only look at the first equation:\n$$H_3PO_4 + H_2O \\rightleftharpoons H_2PO_4^- + H_3O^+$$\n\nThis is a classic buffer solution containing a weak acid ($H_3PO_4$) and its conjugate base ($H_2PO_4^-$, which comes from the potassium salt). \n\n**Step 1: Write the equilibrium expression for $K_{a1}$**\n$$K_{a1} \u003d \\frac{[H_3O^+][H_2PO_4^-]}{[H_3PO_4]}$$\n\n**Step 2: Rearrange to solve for $[H_3O^+]$**\n$$[H_3O^+] \u003d K_{a1} \\times \\frac{[H_3PO_4]}{[H_2PO_4^-]}$$\n*(Note: This is just a rearranged version of the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation!)*\n\n**Step 3: Plug in the given concentrations**\n*   $[H_3PO_4]$ (fosforna kislina) \u003d **2.00 M**\n*   $[H_2PO_4^-]$ (from kalijev dihidrogenfosfat) \u003d **1.50 M**\n*   $K_{a1} \u003d \\mathbf{7.11 \\times 10^{-3}}$\n\n$$[H_3O^+] \u003d (7.11 \\times 10^{-3}) \\times \\frac{2.00}{1.50}$$\n\n**Step 4: Calculate the final answer**\n$$[H_3O^+] \u003d (7.11 \\times 10^{-3}) \\times 1.333$$\n**$[H_3O^+] \u003d 9.48 \\times 10^{-3} \\text{ M}$**\n\n***\n\n### A tiny technical detail (for advanced classes)\nThe calculation above uses the \"approximation method\" (assuming the concentrations of 2.00 M and 1.50 M don\u0027t change at all when reaching equilibrium). \n\nBecause $K_{a1}$ is slightly on the larger side for a weak acid ($10^{-3}$), some very strict professors might want you to use a full ICE table to solve a quadratic equation:\n$7.11 \\times 10^{-3} \u003d \\frac{(x)(1.50 + x)}{2.00 - x}$\n\nIf you solve that quadratic, you get $x \u003d 9.38 \\times 10^{-3} \\text{ M}$. \n\nAs you can see, the difference between the simple way ($9.48 \\times 10^{-3}$) and the brutally hard quadratic way ($9.38 \\times 10^{-3}$) is incredibly small. Unless your professor explicitly demands that you use the quadratic formula for $K_a \u003e 10^{-4}$, **stick to the simple 4-step method above.**",

      "text": "Don\u0027t let the name scare you! An **ICE table** is just a simple bookkeeping system to keep track of concentrations in a chemical reaction.\n\nThink of it like a **bank statement** for your molecules: \n*   **I**nitial: How much \"money\" (concentration) do you have at the start?\n*   **C**hange: How much did you \"spend\" or \"earn\" (react) during the reaction?\n*   **E**quilibrium: How much is left in your account at the end?\n\nHere is how it works with a simple example: a **Weak Acid ($HA$)** dissolving in water.\n\n---\n\n### 1. The Setup\nImagine you have $0.10\\text{ M}$ of a weak acid. The reaction is:\n$$HA \\rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$$\n\nYou set up your table like this:\n\n| | $HA$ | $\\rightleftharpoons$ | $H^+$ | $A^-$ |\n| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |\n| **I** (Initial) | $0.10$ | | $0$ | $0$ |\n| **C** (Change) | $-x$ | | $+x$ | $+x$ |\n| **E** (Equilibrium) | $0.10 - x$ | | $x$ | $x$ |\n\n### 2. What the rows mean:\n*   **Initial:** Before any acid breaks apart, you have the full $0.10\\text{ M}$ of the acid and zero products.\n*   **Change:** Some amount (we call it **$x$**) of the acid breaks apart. Since $HA$ is being \"spent,\" it is **$-x$**. Since the products are being \"earned,\" they are **$+x$**.\n*   **Equilibrium:** You just add the first two rows together. This is the \"final balance\" in your beaker.\n\n### 3. Turning it into Math:\nNow you take the **E** (Equilibrium) values and plug them into your $K_a$ formula:\n$$K_a \u003d \\frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]} \\longrightarrow K_a \u003d \\frac{(x)(x)}{0.10 - x}$$\n\n---\n\n### The \"Good News\" (Why you don\u0027t always need it)\nIn many of the problems we just did, we used **shortcuts** to avoid doing this table every time.\n\n1.  **The \"Buffer\" Shortcut:** If you have a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base (like the phosphoric acid problem), you use the **Henderson-Hasselbalch** equation. That equation is actually just a pre-solved ICE table!\n    $$pH \u003d pK_a + \\log\\left(\\frac{[\\text{base}]}{[\\text{acid}]}\\right)$$\n\n2.  **The \"Small x\" Shortcut:** If the acid is very weak ($K_a$ is very small), then $0.10 - x$ is basically still just $0.10$. This saves you from having to use the quadratic formula.\n\n3.  **The \"Amphoteric\" Shortcut:** In that last problem (Problem 10), the ICE table would be a nightmare because $HA^-$ reacts with itself. That’s why we used the $pH \u003d \\frac{pK_{a1} + pK_{a2}}{2}$ trick instead.\n\n**Summary:** \nICE tables are for when you are **stuck** and don\u0027t have a shortcut. If you know you are at an equivalence point or you have a buffer, **use the shortcuts** and keep the ICE table in your pocket for emergencies! \n\nDoes that make it feel a little less like a \"sob\" moment? :)",

        "text": " (Initial) | $0.10$ | | $0$ | $0$ |\n| **C** (Change) |"
      }, {
        "text": " $-x$ | | $+x$ | $+x$ |\n| **E** (Equilibrium) | $"
      }, {
        "text": "0.10 - x$ | | $x$ | $x$ |\n\n### 2. What the rows mean:\n*"
      }, {
        "text": "   **Initial:** Before any acid breaks apart, you have the full $0.10\\text{ M}$ of"
      }, {
        "text": " the acid and zero products.\n*   **Change:** Some amount (we call it **$x$**) of"
      }, {
        "text": " the acid breaks apart. Since $HA$ is being \"spent,\" it is **$-x$**. Since the products"
      }, {
        "text": " are being \"earned,\" they are **$+x$**.\n*   **Equilibrium:** You just add the first"
      }, {
        "text": " two rows together. This is the \"final balance\" in your beaker.\n\n### 3. Turning it into Math:"
      }, {
        "text": "\nNow you take the **E** (Equilibrium) values and plug them into your $K_a$ formula"
      }, {
        "text": ":\n$$K_a \u003d \\frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]} \\longrightarrow K_a \u003d \\frac{("
      }, {
        "text": "x)(x)}{0.10 - x}$$\n\n---\n\n### The \"Good News\" (Why you don\u0027t always"
      }, {
        "text": " need it)\nIn many of the problems we just did, we used **shortcuts** to avoid doing this table every time.\n\n"
      }, {
        "text": "1.  **The \"Buffer\" Shortcut:** If you have a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base (like the phosphoric acid problem"
      }, {
        "text": "), you use the **Henderson-Hasselbalch** equation. That equation is actually just a pre-solved ICE table!\n"
      }, {
        "text": "    $$pH \u003d pK_a + \\log\\left(\\frac{[\\text{base}]}{[\\text{acid}]}\\"
      }, {
        "text": "right)$$\n\n2.  **The \"Small x\" Shortcut:** If the acid is very weak ($K_a$ is very"
      }, {
        "text": " small), then $0.10 - x$ is basically still just $0.10$. This saves you from having to use"
      }, {
        "text": " the quadratic formula.\n\n3.  **The \"Amphoteric\" Shortcut:** In that last problem (Problem 10), the ICE"
      }, {
        "text": " table would be a nightmare because $HA^-$ reacts with itself. That’s why we used the $pH \u003d \\frac{pK"
      }, {
        "text": "_{a1} + pK_{a2}}{2}$ trick instead.\n\n**Summary:** \nICE tables"
      }, {
        "text": " are for when you are **stuck** and don\u0027t have a shortcut. If you know you are at an"
      }, {
        "text": " equivalence point or you have a buffer, **use the shortcuts** and keep the ICE table in your pocket for emergencies! "
      }, {
        "text": "\n\nDoes that make it feel a little less like a \"sob\" moment? :)"
      }, {
        "text": "",
        "thoughtSignature": ""
      }],

The Equation\n$$pH \u003d pKa + \\log\\left(\\frac{n_{\\text{base}}}{n_{\\text{acid}}}\\right)$$\n\n*(Note: You can use moles instead of concentration inside the log because the volumes are the same and they just cancel out. The Math\n$$pH \u003d 3.74 + \\log\\left(\\frac{0.228}{0.400}\\right)$$\n$$pH \u003d 3.74 + \\log(0.57)$$\n$$pH \u003d 3.74 - 0.244$$\n**$pH \\approx 3.50$**\n\n**You nailed it.** Once you identify that you have a \"weak acid + its salt,\" the H-H equation is your best friend.
